options.text: Keeping conditions inside the body steady within set limits
options.explanation: Homeostasis is the maintenance of constant internal conditions.
The body cannot alter its surroundings; it regulates its own interior.
Growth is a different life process entirely.
Reproduction has nothing to do with internal regulation.

questions.stem: Which pair names the two examples of homeostasis required by the specification?

options.explanation: Glucose control exists but the specification's pair is temperature and water content.

options.text: Body temperature and body water content
options.explanation: These are the two named homeostatic examples.
Both are responses, not the named homeostatic pair.
Real physiological variables but not the specification's pair.

questions.stem: Why can drifting beyond homeostatic limits be fatal?

options.text: Because receptors run out of stimuli
options.explanation: Receptors do not consume stimuli.
Effectors respond to instructions; this is not the lethal mechanism.

options.text: Because enzymes stop functioning properly outside narrow ranges
options.explanation: Enzyme activity depends on stable internal conditions.

options.text: Because the body immediately runs out of water
options.explanation: Water loss matters but the fatal mechanism is enzyme and cell failure.

questions.stem: Homeostatic control in humans is best described as which kind of process?

options.text: A learned habit trained over years
options.explanation: It is built in from birth, not learned.

options.text: A purely chemical process with no control step
options.explanation: Control systems with receptors and centres are involved.

options.text: A conscious decision made by the thinking brain
options.explanation: You never consciously choose to regulate temperature or water.
Homeostasis runs automatically via the brain stem and spinal cord.

questions.stem: What happens to enzyme activity if the internal environment stays within its set limits?

options.text: It works at its optimum for the organism's cells
options.explanation: Stable conditions are exactly what optimal enzyme and cell function need.
Enzymes always depend on temperature; stability protects that dependence.
Enzyme activity plateaus; limits prevent damage, not boost it.
That is the consequence of exceeding limits, not staying inside them.

questions.modelAnswer: The maintenance of steady internal conditions within narrow set limits.

questions.stem: Name the brain region that monitors the temperature of the blood.
questions.modelAnswer: The thermoregulatory centre, found at the base of the brain.

questions.stem: Explain why any rise or fall in core temperature demands a co-ordinated response.
questions.modelAnswer: Because a temperature shift of more than about two degrees can be fatal: enzymes would no longer function at their optimum, so cooling or heating responses must be coordinated quickly to bring the temperature back toward its set point.

questions.stem: During a heatwave a walker sweats heavily for hours. Name the organ that will adjust the final water balance and outline what it can control.
questions.modelAnswer: The kidneys adjust the balance: water lost through sweat and breathing cannot be controlled, so the kidneys vary how much water is reabsorbed from the filtrate, producing either dilute or concentrated urine to protect the blood's water content.

questions.stem: At approximately what core temperature is human blood held?

options.explanation: Room temperature is not body temperature.
The core is kept close to 37 °C.
That is five degrees low; enzymes would struggle.
That is dangerously high and outside the limits.

questions.stem: Which water loss can the body actually control?

options.explanation: Lung loss is unavoidable.
Sweating serves temperature control; its water cost is not adjustable.
The kidneys control urine volume, making this the adjustable loss.
Tears are negligible and not a named control route.

questions.stem: Where in the nephron is water reabsorbed from the filtrate?

options.explanation: The bladder stores urine; it does not reabsorb water.
The urethra only carries urine out.
Sweat glands are skin structures outside the nephron entirely.
Reabsorption happens specifically from the collecting ducts.

questions.stem: When blood water falls too low, what does the body do?

options.text: Reabsorbs more water, producing a small volume of concentrated urine
options.explanation: More reabsorption conserves water and concentrates the urine.

options.text: Reabsorbs less water, producing dilute urine
options.explanation: That response would worsen the shortage.
Urine production continues, just reduced in volume.

options.text: Increases sweating to cool the blood
options.explanation: Sweating would lose still more water.

questions.stem: Which hormone controls how much water the kidneys reabsorb?

options.explanation: FSH acts in the reproductive system.
ADH controls the reabsorption of water in the nephron.
Insulin manages blood glucose, not water.
Adrenaline prepares the body for emergencies.

questions.stem: State where the thermoregulatory centre is located.
questions.modelAnswer: At the base of the brain.

questions.stem: Name the hormone that controls water reabsorption and the structure where it acts.
questions.modelAnswer: ADH, acting on the collecting ducts of the nephron.

questions.stem: Explain why water lost through the lungs cannot be regulated by the body.
questions.modelAnswer: Breathing must continue constantly to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide, so the water vapour exhaled with each breath is an unavoidable cost — unlike urine, its volume cannot be adjusted without stopping the gas exchange the body needs every second.

questions.stem: A patient drinks a very large volume of water in a short time. Describe what their kidneys should produce and name the hormone change involved.
questions.modelAnswer: With blood water too high, less water is reabsorbed from the filtrate, so the kidneys produce a large volume of dilute urine; ADH levels fall, opening the collecting-duct tap so the excess water leaves the body.
